newsitem.title: UK: Britain cuts cash drain with tax crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Britain cuts cash drain with tax crackdown.

text.p: The British government, worried about a drain on its finances, on Tuesday plugged a tax loophole giving generous tax benefits to shareholders of companies offering share buyback schemes.

The news came just one day before shareholders at international news and information group Reuters Holdings Plc were due to vote on a 613 million pound ($958 million) share buyback. The company promptly put its plans on hold.

Responding to a flood of company buybacks granting tax benefits to big shareholders, the government said such shareholders would no longer be able to claim tax credits on share buyacks or special dividend payouts.
Following the government move, Reuters said it would ask shareholders to adjourn consideration of its share buyback proposals at an extraordinary meeting on Wednesday.

Reuters said it regretted the British government had proposed amendments to the its tax legislation which would apparently make it more difficult for British firms to return cash to shareholders "in a tax neutral way".

Given the uncertainty created by the government's announcement, Reuters believed it was imprudent to proceed without full details of proposed new government legislation. But it would continue to review the options open to it.
Tax experts, describing the government's decision as too harsh, said the timing of its announcement appeared directly related to the Reuters share buyback scheme.
"The timing is no coincidence...it's crystal clear that it's aimed at Reuters special dividend shares," said Roger Muray, tax partner at Ernst & Young.
The government made clear on Tuesday it was scrapping the tax credit scheme to cap a drain on its own finances after a rash of companies had announced buybacks with tax credits.
British finance minister Kenneth Clarke referred to "...the growing loss of tax through schemes involving companies buying their own shares or paying special dividends."

The Treasury's Financial Secretary, Michael Jack, told Reuters the cost of companies taking advantage of tax credits on share buybacks had risen to an unacceptable level and the government had been considering tax changes since last year.
"Then the number of people using this scheme was very much at the level of the trickle, but the trickle has turned into something of a river," Jack said.

So far this year British firms have announced plans to spend up to 2.5 billion pounds ($4 billion) in buying back their own shares. The total had been expected to rise to four billion pounds by the end of the year.
Share buybacks are most beneficial to tax-exempt shareholders, principally pension funds, which can claim tax credits from the government.

Although Reuters said it would adjourn a decision on its own share buyback scheme, British bank Barclays Plc said the government ruling would not affect its plans for further repurchases of its own stock.

The government news initially sent shock waves through the stock market, depressing not only Reuters shares but prices of other stocks, like banks and utilities, which were expected to launch share buyback schemes.
But tax experts later concluded that companies would still be able to find other ways of returning excess cash to shareholders and the market later settled down.
Reuters shares ended the day down 20-1/2 pence at 756-1/2 pence, after earlier hitting a low of 750. ($1=.6401 Pound)
